## Does the Net Still Route Around Censorship? {.center}

> "The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it."
> — John Gilmore, *Time*, December 6, 1993

We opened the term on this line. Today: was it right, and what changed?

::: {.notes}
- Same quote as Meeting 1. Ask for a show of hands: true in 1993? true now?
- Your answer, in your own words: where it still holds (protocols, VPNs, Tor) and where it stopped holding.
- Shape of today: look back, the central questions, where control is heading, who decides, then back to the breakouts.
:::

# Looking Back

## A Tax on Access

- Blocking is the crudest form; the broader idea is anything that makes
  information **harder to get**
- Roberts, *Censored* (2018): **fear · friction · flooding**
- Blocking is visible and provokes a reaction; friction and flooding often go
  unnoticed
- Not only authoritarian states: democracies throttle, take down, and shut down
  too

::: {.notes}
- The Meeting 1 framing. Restate it as you would now, after the term.
- Roberts's 2014 Instagram example (Meeting 8): blocking pushed people to VPNs; flooding leaves nothing to circumvent.
- Ask: by the end of the term, which of the three did we see most of?
- Book: Ch. 1.
:::

## The Term in Five Parts {.smaller}

| Part | What we covered | Meetings |
|---|---|---|
| **Technical** | DNS, transport, routes, throttling, denial of service | 2–6 |
| **Platform** | Flooding, disinformation, moderation, personalization | 7–10 |
| **Legal and economic** | Copyright, AI and copyright, net neutrality, zero rating, demonetization | 11–13 |
| **Measurement** | Technical measurement, transparency reports, legal and economic | 14–16 |
| **Taking back control** | VPNs, Tor, countering platform, legal, and economic controls | 17–18, week 9 |

::: {.notes}
- One sentence per row on what you want students to remember.
- Point out the drift across the term: from the network toward platforms, law, and money.
- Book: Ch. 2–6.
:::

## Threads That Ran All Term

- **Who decides?** Cloudflare's Project Galileo; the DoH resolver; the RPKI root;
  GIFCT's hash database
- **Can you even tell?** Throttling vs. congestion; shadowbans; what
  personalization never shows you
- **The path of least resistance.** Censors move to whatever is cheapest:
  technical, legal, or economic
- **AI on both sides.** Cheaper flooding, automated moderation, agents that
  read the web for us

::: {.notes}
- These came out of the reading responses, not the syllabus. Credit the class.
- Who decides: Meeting 6 (Galileo, "imagine being the Cloudflare employee"), Meeting 2 (DoH concentration), Meeting 4 (RPKI root could revoke an AS), Meeting 9 (GIFCT).
- Can you tell: Meeting 5 (throttling is insidious because it is hard to tell from ordinary failure), Meeting 9 (shadowbans hard to prove), Meeting 10 (omissions).
- Path of least resistance: the Meeting 3 breakout report-back on the cat-and-mouse game.
- AI on both sides: Meeting 9's "AI cats and AI mice."
:::

## Measurement Is How We Know

- Without measurement: no extent, no accountability, no way to evaluate a
  countermeasure
- Technical: OONI, Censored Planet, Wehe (our Meeting 5 hands-on)
- Platform: transparency reports, and now **researcher data access** under the
  EU DSA (Art. 40)
- Hard cases stay hard: legitimate variation in DNS answers, personalization,
  congestion that looks like throttling

::: {.vignette}
**DSA data access, slowly.** The delegated act on vetted-researcher access was
published in **July 2025**. By **May 19, 2026**, national coordinators had
received **49 applications**, mostly for social-media data, and were still
assessing them (European Commission).
:::

::: {.notes}
- Tie to the Meeting 2 discussion: detecting DNS manipulation when answers legitimately vary.
- Ask: what would you measure first if you had DSA access tomorrow?
- Book: Ch. 5.
:::

# The Central Questions

## Two Questions from the Start of the Course {.center}

1. To what extent is an **ISP or platform responsible** for the speech it
   carries?
2. To what extent is the **cost of Internet access** a financial nudge toward
   certain content?

And one the class added: **who checks the people who decide?**

::: {.notes}
- These two questions have opened and closed my legal and economic lecture for years. Say why you started there.
- The third came from the reading responses all term ("who sets the rules," Meeting 9).
- The next three slides take them one at a time.
:::

## Intermediaries Hold the Switch

- **Private power, no constitution:** when a CDN, cloud, app store, or resolver
  drops you, the effect can match a state block
- Cloudflare and the Daily Stormer (Aug 2017): "No one should have that power"
- Project Galileo: free DDoS protection, if Cloudflare decides you qualify
- Consolidation raises the **blast radius**: the Cloudflare (Nov 18, 2025) and
  AWS us-east-1 (Oct 20, 2025) outages, both self-inflicted, took large parts of
  the web down

::: {.notes}
- Gilmore's line holds at the protocol layer; above it, a few companies became chokepoints.
- Neither outage was an attack: Cloudflare was an oversized Bot Management feature file after a database permissions change; AWS was a race condition in DynamoDB's DNS automation. Ask: if an accident can do this, what could an order do?
- Meeting 4 breakout: should an ISP refuse a shutdown order? Same question for these companies.
- Book: 2.3.2 (Galileo), 3.6.
:::

## Price Is a Filter

- **Zero rating:** free access to some apps, metered access to the rest
  - Our Kenya and South Africa work: walled garden or gateway?
  - India barred discriminatory data tariffs (2016), ending Free Basics there
- **Paywalls:** hard and soft paywalls decide who reads the news (Meeting 6)
- **Tiered AI:** do paid models answer what free tiers refuse? (Meeting 7)
- **Demonetization:** speech stays up but stops paying

::: {.notes}
- This is question 2. Talk through your own zero-rating findings: WhatsApp on Cell C, Twitter on MTN in 2014, and the survey result that most users who started on zero-rated apps moved to paid plans.
- Paywalls: the soft-paywall point from Meeting 6, built so search engines (and now agents) see the full text.
- Tiered AI was deferred from Meeting 7 to the economic-controls meeting; close the loop here.
- Book: 4.3–4.4.
:::

## The Law Sets the Defaults

- **Section 230** and the **DMCA** safe harbor: immunity, conditioned on
  behavior
- Notice and takedown is asymmetric: a web form on one side, a sworn statement
  and legal risk on the other
- A takedown reversed two weeks later can still have worked (Meeting 11)
- **SLAPPs** and the **CFAA** chill speech and research (*Sandvig v. Barr*)
- "Kill switch" bills recur in the U.S.; none has become law

::: {.notes}
- Question 1 from the legal side. Ask: what did the safe harbors get right in 1996–98, and what do they get wrong now?
- Your own SLAPP example (the review and the demand letter) from Meeting 11.
- Kill switch: my old slide asked whether a "national cyberemergency" shutdown makes technical sense. Ask it again after the BGP and shutdown material.
- Book: 4.1–4.2.
:::

# Where Control Is Heading

## AI as Arbiter

- Chatbots and AI search now decide what you see, and what they **refuse**
- Refusals are opaque: system prompts, post-training, and policy choices are not
  public
- Models disagree with each other on what is allowed
- Agents read the web for us: does throttling still work if an agent fetches
  overnight from a cache?

::: {.notes}
- Meeting 7 responses: should an AI system have to say which policy caused a refusal?
- Meetings 5–6: if friction stops working because agents prefetch, does censorship swing back toward blocking? Agents can themselves be throttled or blocked.
- Mention the PhD project on whether people in different regions get different information through agents and retrieval.
- Book: 3.6, 3.7.
:::

## AI as Content

- LLMs make flooding cheap: fake accounts, matched writing styles, synthetic
  media
- "Dead internet": how much of what you see is bots talking to bots?
- Detection is a cat-and-mouse game, automated on both sides
- Provenance helps a little: it proves who signed, not what is true

::: {.vignette}
**Labels are now law in the EU.** AI Act **Art. 50** transparency duties
(chatbot disclosure, deepfake labels) apply from **Aug 2, 2026**. The Digital
Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744, in force **July 27, 2026**) delayed high-risk rules to
Dec 2027 but not Art. 50; machine-readable marking gets a grace period, only for
systems already on the market, to **Dec 2, 2026**. Google's Pixel 10 (Aug 2025)
signs every camera photo with C2PA Content Credentials.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Meeting 8: LLMs bring the cost of flooding down; nobody had a clean answer on what to do about it.
- Meeting 12 hands-on: did the AI image carry C2PA provenance? What did students find?
- Ask: is a label a form of information control?
- Book: 3.1–3.5, 4.2.
:::

## Gates at the Front Door: Age Verification

- Meeting 1 breakout: is age verification a form of information control?
- U.S.: *Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton* (June 27, 2025, 6–3) upheld Texas's
  age checks for adult sites
- Australia: under-16 social media minimum age from **Dec 10, 2025**; platforms
  restricted **4.7 million** accounts in the first weeks (eSafety, Jan 2026)
- Same failure mode as a spam filter: a wrong guess removes a legitimate speaker

::: {.vignette}
**Freedom on the Net 2026** (Freedom House, **Oct 22, 2026**): internet freedom
declined for the **16th straight year**; **10 of 38** countries assessed had
proposed, passed, or implemented age-assurance laws; Iran imposed a nationwide
shutdown of about **88 days**, the longest the report has recorded.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Close the loop on the very first breakout. Has anyone changed their answer?
- Privacy and ID requirements for minors came up in the Meeting 1 report-back.
- Freedom House paused coverage of 34 countries this year after funding cuts, so 38 countries instead of the usual seventy-odd. Measurement itself depends on funding.
- Book: Ch. 1, 4.1.
:::

## Encryption at Both Ends {.smaller}

- **The network:** encrypted DNS and ECH hide what you visit; censors attack
  the weakest link instead
  - GFW has blocked QUIC by SNI since **Apr 7, 2024**; quic-go v0.52.0 shipped
    SNI slicing **May 23, 2025**
  - Jan 2025: GFW not blocking ECH unless the outer SNI is blocked; Uzbekistan
    blocked QUIC with ECH (Dec 2024)
- **The endpoint:** EU "Chat Control"
  - Council dropped mandatory scanning (Nov 2025); trilogues continue, next
    round scheduled **Dec 8, 2026**
  - Voluntary scanning lapsed in Apr 2026, then was extended to Apr 2028 (July
    2026)

::: {.notes}
- Network side: Meeting 2 (DoH) and Meeting 3 (fingerprinting). The censor doesn't break the crypto; it goes after the bootstrap, the fingerprint, or the IP.
- Endpoint side: if you can't read the wire, scan the phone. Ask: is client-side scanning censorship, surveillance, or both?
- The Dec 8 trilogue lands right after this lecture. Say what you expect.
- Book: 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 6.1.
:::

## Shutdowns and Fragmentation

- The bluntest tool keeps growing: **313 shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025**
  (Access Now, Mar 31, 2026), up from 304 in 2024
  - Myanmar 95, India 65; conflict the leading trigger (125)
  - 14 disruptions of satellite internet, up from 4
- Sovereign networks: Russia's 2019 law and DPI mandates; China's firewall
- Data localization: the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework survived *Latombe*
  (Sept 3, 2025) and is on appeal (C-703/25 P)

::: {.notes}
- Meeting 4: withdrawing BGP routes is how a country disappears. The breakout asked whether an ISP should refuse.
- Satellite: people assumed Starlink routes around shutdowns; the count says governments go after it too.
- Ask whether one global Internet is still the default, or a policy choice some countries have opted out of.
- Book: 2.2.3, 4.1.
:::

# Who Decides?

## Governance Was Never Absent {.smaller}

> "the development and application by Governments, the private sector and civil
> society, in their respective roles, of shared principles, norms, rules,
> decision-making procedures, and programmes that shape the evolution and use of
> the Internet."
> — WSIS, Tunis Agenda (2005)

- Multistakeholder (ICANN, IETF, RIRs) vs. multilateral (ITU, "cyber
  sovereignty")
- `.io`: UK–Mauritius Chagos treaty signed May 22, 2025, ratification frozen in
  2026; `.io` still active

::: {.notes}
- The technical community made governance decisions all term: DoH defaults, RPKI, QUIC.
- .io: a geopolitical deal decides the fate of a namespace with more than a million registrations. Ask who should have a say.
:::

## Platform Governance Experiments

- **Meta's Oversight Board:** **347** recommendations through June 2026, **214**
  implemented (Meta, H1 2026); funding extended through 2028 (May 2026)
- **Community Notes:** crowd fact-checks, often after the post has gone viral
- **Bluesky labelers / Mastodon federation:** choose your moderator
- **Law:** EU DSA risk assessments and data access; national takedown laws

::: {.notes}
- Meeting 9: notes arrive late; note-writers can be biased or coordinate.
- Ask: is a board funded by the company it oversees independent? Is "choose your moderator" just personalization again (Meeting 10)?
- Book: 3.6.
:::

## One Network, Many Laws

- Right to be forgotten: *Google Spain* (2014); limited to the EU (*Google v.
  CNIL*, 2019)
- Australia v. X (2024): can one country order a global takedown?
- India's IT Rules (2021): traceability and fast takedowns
- Every platform rule is applied to billions of people across dozens of legal
  regimes

::: {.notes}
- Ask: should the strictest country's law win, the platform's home country's, or the user's?
- Connect to the gap the Meeting 11 responses noticed: international copyright and jurisdiction.
- Book: 4.1.
:::

# Taking Back Control

## Levers That Exist

- **Technical:** circumvention (VPNs, Tor, pluggable transports), encrypted DNS,
  ECH, padding
- **Measurement:** public data that makes control visible and costly
- **Legal:** challenges, data access, limits on intermediary liability,
  anti-SLAPP laws
- **Economic:** competition, interoperability, choice of ranking
- **Individual:** knowing it is happening, and noticing what is missing

::: {.notes}
- Detail is in the countering deck (06-Circumvention/02-Countering); here, one sentence on each.
- Meeting 10: a student proposed paying for an algorithm whose goal is navigation, not engagement.
- Ask: which lever do you personally have?
- Book: Ch. 6.
:::

## Back to the Breakouts

- Is the cat-and-mouse game winnable? (Meeting 3)
- Should an ISP refuse a government shutdown order? (Meeting 4)
- Should DDoS protection be a common-carrier obligation? (Meeting 6)
- Is personalization censorship? (Meeting 10)
- Should training a model on a work require a licence? (Meeting 12)

::: {.notes}
- Pick two or three. Ask the room for their answer now, then give yours.
- This is where to say what you actually think; it is the material the conclusion needs.
:::

## What You Carry Out of This Course

- Control is a **spectrum**: blocking, friction, flooding, ranking
- Ask **who decides**, by what process, and who can check them
- Ask **how you would know**: what would you measure?
- Every intervention has a cost on the other side; name it
- The same tools that control can also be used to resist

::: {.notes}
- Say this in your own words; these are prompts, not the list.
- Remind them of their projects: each one measured or tested one of these.
:::

## Does the Net Still Route Around Censorship? {.center}

Where does it still hold? Where did it stop holding?

What would have to change for it to hold again?

::: {.notes}
- Return to the opening show of hands. Give your answer.
- End where you want the conclusion to end.
:::
